training-high.t: Now let the tree grow to **depth 8**. On the data it trained on it reaches **F1 0.97**, which looks excellent. But the training score alone cannot tell us whether it will work on new customers.

validation-lower.t: The yellow line is validation. At depth 8 it falls to **0.59**, lower than the depth-4 tree's **0.676**. Extra flexibility stopped helping on new data.

performance-gap.t: The red bracket marks the gap: **0.97 − 0.59 = 0.38**. Strong on training but much weaker on validation is the signature of **overfitting**. It is evidence, not proof of one particular cause.

complex-model.t: A depth-8 tree can **memorize which of the 700 training customers churned**, including accidental details that do not carry over. Too much flexibility for the data is the classic cause.

leakage-check.t: A leaky feature also gives a **strong training score that collapses elsewhere**. So before blaming complexity, we also check the features and how validation has been used.

regularization.t: **Regularization** penalizes complexity, much as ridge regression penalizes large weights. For a tree, using a smaller depth does the same job.

simpler-model.t: At **depth 4** the scores are **0.76 on training and 0.676 on validation**, a gap of only **0.08**. The simpler model gives up some training score but does better on new data.

new-validation.t: After any change we measure again on **validation data**. The test set is not used to decide, or it would stop being an honest final check.

overfit-summary.t: **Strong on training but much weaker on validation** suggests overfitting. Form a hypothesis, change one thing, and measure on validation again.
